answers.stem_only: Move the S3 download from the handler into the initialization code (outside the handler) so it runs once per execution environment and is reused by later invocations; then configure provisioned concurrency (about 20) on an alias or version and point callers at it, so environments are initialized ahead of time and even the first request in each environment is fast. A /tmp cache inside the handler still makes the first request slow, and a rebuild on containers is more effort.

Set reserved concurrency of 50 on the function. Reserved concurrency is also the maximum, so Lambda throttles invocations above 50 and API Gateway returns an error that the clients already retry; the integration stays synchronous so clients still get the order result. A queue would break the synchronous response, provisioned concurrency does not cap concurrency, and moving to containers adds overhead.

S3 invokes the function asynchronously. Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocation with the separate S3 bucket as the destination: Lambda writes an invocation record with the event and details about the failed invocation (error, request context). To get the record right after the first failure, set the maximum retry attempts of the asynchronous invocation configuration to 0. A dead-letter queue keeps only the event with few details and is a queue, not an S3 object; custom error-handling code is more overhead and misses timeouts.

On the Kinesis event source mapping, turn on bisect batch on function error and set a maximum retry attempts (and/or maximum record age) so a failing batch is eventually skipped and the shard keeps moving; add an on-failure destination that keeps the full record content, which is an Amazon S3 bucket (SQS or SNS destinations receive only metadata about the batch, not the records). A function dead-letter queue applies only to asynchronous invocations, not stream event source mappings.
